questions: Why do societies need rules?
Is it ever acceptable to break a rule you believe is unfair?
Should young people be involved in making the rules that affect them?
Why do some people obey rules even when no one is watching?
Do you think there will be more or fewer rules in society in the future?
sampleAnswers: Essentially, rules allow large numbers of people to live together without constant conflict. They create predictability, so you can drive knowing that others will stop at red lights, or sign a contract knowing it will be honoured. Without them, the strongest or the most aggressive people would tend to get their way. Rules also protect people who might otherwise be vulnerable, such as children, workers or minorities, so they're not only about order but also about fairness.

I think it can be, but only under certain conditions. History has plenty of examples, such as the civil rights movement, where breaking unjust laws was the only way to change them. However, I'd distinguish between that and simply ignoring rules that are inconvenient. If someone breaks a rule openly, for a principled reason, and is prepared to accept the consequences, that seems legitimate to me. Breaking rules secretly for personal advantage is a very different matter.

Yes, I strongly believe they should, at least to some extent. Young people are more likely to respect rules if they understand the reasons behind them and feel they've had a say. Some schools have student councils that discuss things like uniform or phone policies, and in my experience that leads to more sensible rules and fewer conflicts. Obviously adults should keep the final responsibility, especially on safety issues, but consultation costs very little and achieves a lot.

I suppose there are a few explanations. For many people, rules become internalised: they've been brought up to believe that certain behaviour is right, so obeying is a matter of conscience rather than fear. There's also a sense of fairness; if everyone else waits in the queue, it feels wrong to push in. And some people simply prefer the comfort of routine. Interestingly, research suggests that people are much more honest when they feel part of a community.

My guess is that there will be more rules, but of a different kind. New technologies keep creating situations that existing laws don't cover, for instance around artificial intelligence, data privacy and drones, so governments will have to regulate them. At the same time, some older rules, particularly those related to personal lifestyle choices, may continue to relax. So society might become more regulated in technical areas but more tolerant in private matters.

questions: Why do people find it hard to change their opinions?
What is the most effective way to persuade someone to change their mind?
Has social media made people more or less open to different opinions?
Is it a sign of weakness or strength when a politician changes their mind?
Should schools teach students how to debate and argue?
sampleAnswers: A big part of it is identity. Opinions on things like politics or religion are often tied to who we are and which group we belong to, so changing them can feel like betraying friends or family. There's also a well-known psychological tendency to notice evidence that supports what we already believe and dismiss evidence against it. And admitting you were wrong can be embarrassing, particularly if you've argued your position publicly.

In my experience, it's rarely by bombarding them with facts. People tend to become defensive if they feel attacked. It works much better if you start by showing that you understand their point of view, find some common ground, and then perhaps ask questions that lead them to reconsider. Personal stories can also be very powerful, because they appeal to emotions as well as logic. And it helps if the message comes from someone they already trust.

On the whole, I'd say less open, although it didn't have to be that way. In theory, social media exposes us to a far wider range of views than ever before. In practice, algorithms tend to show us content we agree with, and the most extreme or angry posts get the most attention. That creates echo chambers, where people mostly hear their own opinions repeated back to them, and see the other side only in its worst form.

It really depends on why they've changed it. If a politician changes their position because new evidence has emerged, or because circumstances have changed, I think that shows maturity and honesty. The problem is that voters often punish it, calling it a U-turn, which encourages politicians to stick to bad policies. On the other hand, if someone changes their mind simply because opinion polls have shifted, that does suggest a lack of principles.

Definitely. Debating teaches students to research a topic, structure an argument and speak confidently, which are valuable skills in almost any career. Perhaps more importantly, when you have to argue a side you don't personally agree with, you're forced to understand how other people think. That kind of intellectual empathy is in short supply these days, so if schools could cultivate it, I think society would benefit enormously.

questions: What is the difference between constructive criticism and negative criticism?
Why do some people react badly to criticism?
Should teachers focus more on praise or on correcting mistakes?
How has the internet changed the way people give and receive criticism?
Do you think managers should receive feedback from the people who work for them?
sampleAnswers: I'd say constructive criticism is focused on helping the other person improve. It's specific, it's about the work rather than the person, and it usually suggests what could be done differently. Negative criticism, by contrast, tends to be vague or personal, something like saying a piece of work is just bad, and it often seems designed more to make the critic feel superior than to help. The intention behind it makes a huge difference.

Often it's because criticism feels like a threat to their self-esteem, especially if they've invested a lot of time or emotion in something. People who are insecure may hear any criticism as a judgement of their whole worth. Cultural factors play a role too; in some workplaces or families, mistakes are treated as shameful, so people learn to be defensive. And of course, the way the criticism is delivered matters: public or sarcastic criticism is much harder to accept.

I think they need a balance, but praise should probably come first. Students who feel that their efforts are recognised are more willing to take risks and make mistakes, which is how people learn. That said, praise has to be honest and specific; if everything is described as excellent, it becomes meaningless. And correcting mistakes is essential, as long as it's framed as part of the learning process rather than as failure.

It's made criticism far more public and often far harsher. Anyone can leave a review of a restaurant or comment on someone's post, and because people are anonymous or physically distant, they say things they would never say face to face. That can be quite damaging, especially for young people. On the positive side, online reviews have given consumers more power and forced businesses to respond to complaints, so it isn't all bad.

Yes, I think it's very valuable, provided it's done safely. Employees often see problems that managers are completely unaware of, such as unclear instructions or unfair workloads. The difficulty is that people may be afraid of consequences if they're honest, so anonymous surveys usually work better than face-to-face conversations at first. Managers who genuinely act on feedback tend to earn far more respect and loyalty from their teams.

questions: Why do many people find it difficult to be patient nowadays?
Can patience be taught to children? How?
In what jobs is patience particularly important?
Is the expectation of instant results affecting education?
Are there any situations where being impatient is a good thing?
sampleAnswers: I think technology has played a large role. We've become used to getting almost everything instantly, whether it's information, entertainment or a parcel delivered the next day. So when something takes time, like a slow queue or a project that doesn't show results quickly, it feels unusually frustrating. The pace of modern life also means people often feel they don't have time to wait, even when there's no real hurry.

Yes, I'm fairly sure it can, mostly through experience rather than lectures. Activities like gardening, learning an instrument or saving up for something they want show children that effort pays off over time. Parents can also help by not giving in immediately every time a child demands something. And adults set an example: a child who sees their parents losing their temper in traffic will probably learn to do the same.

Teaching is an obvious one, because children learn at very different speeds and need things explained many times. Healthcare is another, particularly nursing and caring for elderly people, who may be confused or slow. I'd also mention scientific research, where experiments often fail for years before producing a result. In all of these, impatience doesn't just make the job unpleasant; it can actually lead to mistakes or harm.

I believe it is, to some extent. Students sometimes expect to master a language or a subject quickly, partly because apps and online courses promise fast results. When they don't see progress, they lose motivation. At the same time, the focus on frequent testing in many schools encourages short-term memorisation rather than deep understanding. Real learning usually involves a period of struggle, and students need to be taught that this is normal.

Definitely. Impatience with injustice or with inefficient systems has driven a lot of positive change. If people had been patient about issues like workers' rights or pollution, many reforms would have taken far longer. In business, too, a degree of impatience can push companies to innovate rather than accepting slow, outdated ways of doing things. The key is to direct that impatience towards problems, not towards other people.

questions: Why are some people more willing to take risks than others?
Do you think young people take more risks than older people? Why?
Are modern societies too focused on safety?
Should governments stop people from doing dangerous activities, such as extreme sports?
What kinds of risks are necessary for a country's economy to grow?
sampleAnswers: It's partly a question of personality; some people seem naturally drawn to excitement and novelty, while others value security. But circumstances matter just as much. Someone with savings, a supportive family or a good education can afford to take risks, because if things go wrong they have something to fall back on. People with dependants or financial difficulties often can't. Previous experience counts too: if you've taken a risk that paid off, you're more likely to try again.

Generally speaking, yes. Part of the explanation is biological; research suggests that the parts of the brain that control impulses aren't fully developed until people reach their mid-twenties. Young people also have fewer responsibilities, so the consequences of failure seem smaller. And there's social pressure, because taking risks can be a way of gaining status among friends. That said, older people take different kinds of risks, such as starting a business or changing career later in life.

In some ways, I think they are. Children today are often not allowed to play outside unsupervised or climb trees, which previous generations did freely, and that may deprive them of the chance to learn how to judge risk for themselves. Workplaces can also be weighed down by excessive health and safety procedures. Of course, many safety measures have saved countless lives, so the challenge is to distinguish between sensible precautions and overprotection.

I don't think they should ban them, as long as the person is an adult and the risk mainly affects themselves. Personal freedom includes the freedom to do things that others consider foolish. However, governments can reasonably insist on safety standards, training or insurance, particularly when rescue services, paid for by taxpayers, may have to get involved. So regulation makes sense, but outright prohibition would be excessive in most cases.

Investment is the obvious one. Entrepreneurs have to risk their own money to start businesses, and investors have to back ideas that might fail, because that's how new industries are created. Governments also need to take some risks, for instance by funding research or new technologies before it's clear they'll succeed. A country where failure is heavily stigmatised, and where people are afraid to try something new, will probably struggle to innovate.

questions: What can older people learn from younger people?
Is the gap between generations bigger now than it was in the past?
Why is it sometimes difficult for adults to learn from children?
How could families and communities encourage more contact between generations?
Do you think traditional knowledge from older generations is being lost?
sampleAnswers: The most obvious example is technology. Younger people are usually much more comfortable with new devices and apps, and they can help older relatives with everything from video calls to online banking. But I think there's more to it than that. Young people are often more open-minded about social issues, and they can challenge assumptions that older people have never questioned. Children in particular can remind adults to be curious and to enjoy things without worrying so much.

In some respects, I think it is. Technology changes so quickly now that a twenty-year-old and a sixty-year-old can live in almost completely different digital worlds, using different platforms and even different ways of communicating. Economic differences matter too: in many countries, young people find it much harder to buy a home than their parents did, which can create resentment. On the other hand, families are often closer emotionally than in the past, so it's not all division.

Partly it's a question of status. Adults are used to being the ones who know more, so accepting that a child understands something better can feel uncomfortable or even humiliating. There's also an assumption that children's ideas are naive. And practically speaking, children don't usually explain things in a structured way; they just do them, so adults have to be willing to observe and ask questions rather than expect a lesson.

There are some lovely initiatives already. Some care homes share their space with nurseries, so elderly residents and toddlers spend time together, which seems to benefit both groups. Schools could invite grandparents to talk about history or teach traditional skills, while teenagers could volunteer to teach digital skills at community centres. Within families, I think simple things help a lot, such as regular shared meals where everyone, whatever their age, is expected to take part in the conversation.

To some degree, yes. Skills such as preserving food, repairing clothes or traditional crafts are no longer passed down automatically, because families live further apart and people can buy almost everything cheaply. Local dialects and oral stories are disappearing in many places too. That said, there's been a revival of interest in some of these things, partly thanks to the internet, where people share recipes and techniques. So the way knowledge is transmitted has changed, but it hasn't disappeared entirely.
